title: Running TypeScript on Node

story: For years your TypeScript has run in a browser, and Vite stood between your code and the browser. It removed the types, found your files when you left out the ending of an import, and your editor drew a red line under every mistake. Your first job on the agent platform is different: a small piece of a Node service that turns a Jira ticket into the name of Nova's branch. Nova is our agent that turns a ticket into a pull request, and it pushes its work to a branch called nova/ plus the ticket key.

You write the helper, run it, and it prints nova/undefined. No error, no warning: you typed ticket.jiraKey where the object has ticket.key, and nothing stopped it. You fix that, it works on your laptop, and the next morning the same service crashes on start in its Docker image with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND, because one import has no .js at the end.
hook.question: Without Vite in the middle, which tool runs my TypeScript on Node, which tool checks it, and what must the project look like so the same code works on my laptop, in CI and in production?

read.h: Node runs JavaScript, so something must remove the types
p: Node is the JavaScript engine from Chrome without the browser around it. Instead of the DOM it gives you modules for files, processes and the network, and it runs on servers, in containers and on Nova's machines. Like the browser, it does not understand TypeScript. Something has to remove the types before Node runs the code, and in the frontend that something is Vite.

On our platform, during development and in tests, it is tsx: a small tool that takes a .ts file, removes the types and runs the result at once. Notice the word removes. tsx never checks a type, which is exactly why it is fast, and exactly why nothing stopped ticket.jiraKey: to tsx it is just a property that happens to be undefined.

Every platform package is also an ES module, which means its files use import and export, like your frontend code. Node decides this per package: "type": "module" in package.json switches it on. Without that line Node treats .js files as the older CommonJS style, with require(), and the imports in the built files fail.

code.text:
mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/p1-1 && cd ~/academy-labs/p1-1
npm init -y > /dev/null
npm pkg set type=module
printf 'save-exact=true\n' > .npmrc
npm install -D typescript@5.9.3 tsx@4.20.3 @types/node@24.12.2

notes.text: Every .js file in this package is now an ES module: import and export, never require.
From now on npm writes exact versions, such as 5.9.3 instead of ^5.9.3. The last section explains why.
The compiler, the runner, and the types for Node's own modules (process, node:fs and the rest). They are dev tools, so -D.

added 8 packages, and audited 9 packages in 4s
found 0 vulnerabilities

deeper.h: Go deeper: Node can remove types by itself now
p: Since Node 22.18 and in Node 24, node src/main.ts works without any tool: Node strips simple types itself. It still checks nothing, it refuses a few TypeScript features that need real code to be generated (enums, for example), and it loads exactly the path you import. So an import of ./branch.js fails when only branch.ts exists, because Node does not map .js to .ts the way tsx does.

That is why the platform keeps tsx for development and tests and runs built JavaScript in production. If Node's own stripping grows up, tsx is the piece we would remove, and nothing else in this lesson would change.

The tool that does check is tsc, the TypeScript compiler, the same program your editor uses for its red lines. It reads tsconfig.json, follows every import and reports every type error. It has two jobs, chosen by one flag. With --noEmit it only checks and writes nothing; we call that typecheck, and CI runs it on every pull request. Without the flag it also writes plain .js files to dist/, and that is the build: a container image runs node dist/main.js, with no TypeScript tools inside.

So the two tools split the work. tsx gives you a fast loop while you work, and tsc is the gate that refuses a mistake before anyone runs the code for real. If you only ever run tsx, you have no type checking at all, however strict your tsconfig is.

notes.text: Every strict check on, as in the frontend: no implicit any, and null is a separate type.
NodeNext tells tsc to follow Node's own rules for modules. The next section shows the rule that causes the most trouble.
An import that brings only types must say import type, so tsc never has to guess which imports to drop.
Load the types of Node (process, Buffer, node:fs) and nothing from the browser, so document is an error here.
The build writes src/main.ts to dist/main.js.
Check only the files in src/ and what they import.

read.see:
$ npx tsx src/main.ts
Nova will push to nova/undefined
$ npx tsc --noEmit
src/main.ts(4,51): error TS2339: Property 'jiraKey' does not exist on type '{ key: string; summary: string; }'.

read.h: An import names the file that will run
p: The crash in the image came from one import. In the frontend you write import { branchFor } from "./branch" and Vite finds branch.ts. Node does not guess: it loads exactly the path you wrote. After the build there is no branch.ts any more, only dist/branch.js, so the import has to say ./branch.js, the name of the file that will exist when the code runs. It looks strange the first time, because the file you see in your editor is branch.ts.

This is the rule that "moduleResolution": "NodeNext" teaches tsc. With it, tsc refuses ./branch with error TS2835 and even suggests the fix. tsx, on the other hand, is forgiving and runs ./branch anyway. That forgiveness is how the bug in the story passed on a laptop and failed in the image: only tsc knew, and only node dist/main.js could prove it.

notes.text: The file next to this one is branch.ts. We write .js because that is the file Node loads after the build, and tsx maps it back to branch.ts while you develop.

read.see:
$ npm start   (built with "./branch" and no ending)
Error [ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND]: Cannot find module '.../dist/branch' imported from .../dist/main.js

read.h: One lockfile for many services, and exact versions
p: The platform is several services in one repo: the gateway (our only door to Claude), the broker (our only door to GitHub, Jira and Slack), the orchestrator, the harness that runs on Nova's machine, the Slack app, and a shared package they all use. Each one is an npm workspace, which means a folder with its own package.json, listed in the root package.json. One npm install at the root installs everything into one node_modules, links each workspace there under its name, and writes one package-lock.json. So the broker imports the shared package by its name, with no relative path and nothing published to npm.

Every version is pinned exactly. The .npmrc line save-exact=true makes npm write 5.9.3 instead of ^5.9.3, and the caret is what lets an install quietly take 5.9.4 tomorrow. With exact pins and one lockfile, a dependency only moves when a pull request changes it, and a reviewer sees the change.

code.file: package.json at the root of a workspace repo (shortened)

notes.text: npm refuses to publish a private package, so nobody uploads the platform to the public registry by mistake.
Each name is a folder with its own package.json. npm links them into node_modules by their package names.
Run the typecheck script in every workspace that has one.
Exact versions: no ^ or ~ in front.

p: npm install may update the lockfile when package.json asks for something new. npm ci never does: it deletes node_modules, installs exactly what the lockfile says, and fails if package.json and the lockfile disagree. That is why CI and every Dockerfile use npm ci.

Some packages run their own scripts when they are installed. A hijacked dependency can use that moment to run anything on the build machine, so our builds add --ignore-scripts, and the install runs no code that nobody read.

lab.title: Run, check and build a tiny Node project
needs: Node 22 or newer (the platform runs Node 24)
About 30 MB of disk for the packages
lab.goal: See with your own eyes that tsx runs code with type errors, that tsc catches them, and that a missing .js in an import only breaks the built code.

guess.q: src/main.ts calls branchFor(ticket.jiraKey), but the object only has a key field. You run it with npx tsx src/main.ts. What happens?

options.text: tsx stops with a type error and runs nothing.
options.why: tsx removes types and runs the result. It never checks them, so it has no reason to stop.
To tsx, ticket.jiraKey is just a property that does not exist, so its value is undefined. Only tsc would refuse it.

options.text: Node crashes, because undefined cannot go into a template string.
options.why: JavaScript happily turns undefined into the text "undefined". That is what makes this bug so quiet.

follow.say: Make an empty Node project that uses ES modules and exact versions, and install the three tools.
follow.do: mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/p1-1 && cd ~/academy-labs/p1-1 && npm init -y > /dev/null && npm pkg set type=module && printf 'save-exact=true\n' > .npmrc && npm install -D typescript@5.9.3 tsx@4.20.3 @types/node@24.12.2
follow.see:

2 packages are looking for funding

follow.say: Write the tsconfig, the helper and a main file. main.ts has the typo from the story on purpose.
Run it with tsx, the way you would while working, and see the typo go straight through.
Now let tsc check the same file. Add the three scripts every platform package has, then run the check.
follow.do: npm pkg set scripts.typecheck="tsc --noEmit" scripts.build="tsc" scripts.start="node dist/main.js" && npm run typecheck
follow.see:
> p1-1@1.0.0 typecheck
> tsc --noEmit

src/main.ts(4,51): error TS2339: Property 'jiraKey' does not exist on type '{ key: string; summary: string; }'.

follow.say: Fix the typo, and at the same time remove the .js from the import, the way you would write it in the frontend. tsx still runs it.
follow.do: sed -i.bak 's/ticket.jiraKey/ticket.key/; s#"./branch.js"#"./branch"#' src/main.ts && npx tsx src/main.ts

follow.say: Build it and run the built file, the way a container would. tsc complains but still writes dist/, and Node then fails.
follow.see:
src/main.ts(1,27): error TS2835: Relative import paths need explicit file extensions in ECMAScript imports when '--moduleResolution' is 'node16' or 'nodenext'. Did you mean './branch.js'?
…
> node dist/main.js
Error [ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND]: Cannot find module '…/p1-1/dist/branch' imported from …/p1-1/dist/main.js

follow.say: Put the .js back, build again and run the built file.
follow.do: sed -i.bak 's#"./branch"#"./branch.js"#' src/main.ts && rm -rf dist && npm run build && npm start
follow.see:
> p1-1@1.0.0 build
> tsc

> p1-1@1.0.0 start
> node dist/main.js

Nova will push to nova/RH-1234

lab.build: Turn the folder into a workspace with two packages, like the platform repo. Create shared/package.json with the name @lab/shared, "type": "module" and "exports": "./src/index.ts", and move branchFor into shared/src/index.ts. Add "workspaces": ["shared"] to the root package.json and run npm install. Then change src/main.ts to import branchFor from "@lab/shared" (a package name, so no ending), delete src/branch.ts, and make both npx tsx src/main.ts and npm run typecheck pass.
checks: npx tsx src/main.ts printed nova/undefined while the typo was there, and npm run typecheck reported TS2339 for the same file.
Without the .js ending, npx tsx still ran, but npm start failed with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND.
With the ending back, npm run build && npm start prints Nova will push to nova/RH-1234.
package.json lists typescript, tsx and @types/node with exact versions: no ^ and no ~.
After the build task, ls -l node_modules/@lab/ shows shared -> ../../shared, and npm run typecheck prints no errors.

solution.text:
mkdir -p shared/src
cat > shared/package.json <<'EOF'
{ "name": "@lab/shared", "version": "0.1.0", "type": "module", "exports": "./src/index.ts" }
EOF
echo 'export const branchFor = (jiraKey: string): string => `nova/${jiraKey}`;' > shared/src/index.ts
npm pkg set 'workspaces[0]=shared' && npm install
sed -i.bak 's#"./branch.js"#"@lab/shared"#' src/main.ts && rm src/branch.ts
npx tsx src/main.ts      # Nova will push to nova/RH-1234
npm run typecheck        # no errors

lab.fix: A teammate did not like writing .js in imports, so they changed tsconfig.json to "module": "ESNext" and "moduleResolution": "bundler", the settings a Vite project uses. Now npm run typecheck is clean even with import "./branch", tsx runs fine, and the service crashes on start in its image. Make that change and remove the ending, see typecheck pass and npm start fail, then put NodeNext back and explain why the bundler setting cannot work when Node itself loads the files.
explain: tsx and tsc both read your .ts files. What does each one do with them, and why do we need both?
Why does an import in src/main.ts name ./branch.js when the file next to it is branch.ts?
What does save-exact=true change in package.json, and what problem does that prevent?
lab.done: npm run build && npm start prints Nova will push to nova/RH-1234, and npm run typecheck is clean.

check.q: A teammate says: "We don't need typecheck in CI, tsx already runs every test." What is wrong with that?

options.text: tsx removes types without checking them, so tests can pass while the code has type errors
options.why: tsx only strips the types. A wrong property name, a missing argument or a null that is not handled all run until they cause a visible problem. tsc --noEmit is the only check.

options.text: Nothing is wrong; tsx refuses to run a file with type errors
options.why: That is the common belief, and the lab shows it is false: tsx ran ticket.jiraKey and printed nova/undefined.

options.text: tsx cannot run test files, only main files
options.why: The platform runs every test through tsx. Running is fine; checking is what tsx never does.

check.q: src/main.ts has import { branchFor } from "./branch". It works with tsx on your laptop. What happens when the image runs node dist/main.js?

options.text: It works, because tsc adds the missing .js when it builds
options.why: tsc never rewrites your import paths. It writes them exactly as you wrote them, so dist/main.js still imports ./branch.

options.text: It works, because Node tries .js, .ts and index.js until one exists
options.why: That guessing is what bundlers and the old CommonJS loader do. Node's ES module loader loads exactly the path in the import.

options.text: It crashes with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND, because Node looks for a file called exactly dist/branch
options.why: Only dist/branch.js exists. With NodeNext, tsc would have refused the import with TS2835 before the build ever reached an image.

check.q: Why does the platform pin every dependency to an exact version, such as "zod": "4.6.7"?

options.why: Speed is the same. What changes is who decides when a version moves.

options.text: So a version only changes when a pull request changes it, and a reviewer sees that change
options.why: With ^4.6.7, a fresh install may take 4.7.0 without anyone deciding it. With 4.6.7 and one lockfile, the code that runs is the code that was reviewed.

options.text: npm workspaces only work with exact versions
options.why: Workspaces work with any version ranges. The pins are a choice we make for safety, not something npm requires.

p: The platform repo, ai-agents, has exactly this shape: TypeScript on Node 24, ES modules, one tsconfig.base.json (strict, target ES2023, module and moduleResolution NodeNext, verbatimModuleSyntax) that every package extends, and npm workspaces for shared, gateway, broker, orchestrator, harness and slack-app, each named @rhinohealth/ai-agents-<pkg>. Dependencies are pinned exactly and kept few, as in Byte's repo.
CI runs npm ci, then lint and typecheck in one job and npm test and npm run build in another. Service images run the built dist/ files, and the harness is bundled into one file instead (lesson p1-7).

tickets.why: Creates the ai-agents repo with this exact shape: ESM, NodeNext, npm workspaces, tsx for tests, tsc for typecheck and build, exact pins.
The gateway is the first workspace with real code, run with tsx in tests and built by tsc for its image.

words.plain: A JavaScript file that uses import and export. "type": "module" in package.json makes every .js file in the package one.
A tool that removes the types from a .ts file and runs it at once. It never checks types.
The TypeScript compiler. With --noEmit it only checks; without it, it also writes .js files to dist/.
The tsconfig setting that makes tsc follow Node's own module rules, such as the .js ending on relative imports.
A package inside a bigger repo. One install links all of them by name, with one lockfile.
A dependency written as 4.6.7 instead of ^4.6.7, so it only changes when someone changes it on purpose.

review.q: From memory: the three npm scripts every platform package has, and the command behind each one.
review.a: typecheck runs tsc --noEmit (check only), build runs tsc (check and write dist/), and start runs node dist/main.js (the built code, as in an image). Tests run through tsx.

review.q: A new teammate's import works in dev and crashes in the image with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND. What do you tell them to look for, and which tool would have caught it?
review.a: A relative import without .js. Node loads exactly the path written, and only dist/branch.js exists. tsc with NodeNext refuses it with TS2835, so npm run typecheck catches it before any image is built.

remember: tsx runs your TypeScript without checking it, tsc checks it and builds what Node really runs, so imports name the .js file and versions are pinned exactly.
